studies.title: Cardiac activity appearing in another channel
Slow baseline drift in frontal channels

questions.prompt: Which explanation best fits the abrupt large transient that is isolated mainly to F3-M2?
options: Electrode pop or unstable electrode contact
questions.answer: Electrode pop or unstable electrode contact
questions.rationale: An abrupt nonphysiologic transient that is largely confined to one derivation should prompt a signal-pathway and electrode-contact check before it is interpreted as cerebral activity.

questions.prompt: Which displayed channel contains the strongest abnormal transient?
questions.rationale: The original schematic transient is intentionally concentrated in F3-M2 while neighboring channels remain comparatively stable.

questions.prompt: What is the best next technologist action?
options: Inspect the affected electrode, lead connection, and signal quality before changing interpretation
Immediately score the transient as an arousal
Increase all filter settings until the transient disappears
Ignore it because only one channel is affected
questions.answer: Inspect the affected electrode, lead connection, and signal quality before changing interpretation
questions.rationale: Troubleshooting should follow the signal pathway and correct the source when possible rather than using scoring or filter changes to hide an unstable electrode.

questions.prompt: The repetitive deflections in F3-M2 occur at the same timing as the ECG complexes. What is the most likely explanation?
options: ECG contamination in the EEG derivation
questions.answer: ECG contamination in the EEG derivation
questions.rationale: Time-locking a suspicious waveform to the ECG channel is a strong clue that cardiac activity is contaminating another derivation.

questions.prompt: Which comparison provides the strongest evidence for the artifact source?
options: Compare the suspicious F3-M2 deflections with the ECG channel timing
Change the sleep stage and see whether it disappears
questions.answer: Compare the suspicious F3-M2 deflections with the ECG channel timing
questions.rationale: Cross-channel correlation is central to artifact recognition. Repeated morphology at the same cardiac timing supports ECG contamination.

questions.prompt: What is the best next step after recognizing ECG contamination?
options: Verify the affected electrode pathway and document persistent limitation if it cannot be corrected
Score every contaminating deflection as an EEG event
Apply maximum filtering without checking the electrode pathway
questions.answer: Verify the affected electrode pathway and document persistent limitation if it cannot be corrected
questions.rationale: Correct the technical source when possible and preserve the true ECG channel for clinical monitoring rather than hiding the problem with indiscriminate filtering.

questions.prompt: The very slow, broad baseline shifts are strongest in the frontal derivations and do not behave like organized physiologic slow waves. What is the best artifact label?
questions.rationale: Very slow drifting potentials affecting selected electrodes can mimic slow activity. Distribution and physiologic context help separate artifact from sleep-stage evidence.

questions.prompt: Which observation should make you cautious about calling this normal N3 slow-wave activity?
options: The drift is strongest in selected frontal electrodes without a convincing matching physiologic pattern across the epoch
The patient has an ECG channel
questions.answer: The drift is strongest in selected frontal electrodes without a convincing matching physiologic pattern across the epoch
questions.rationale: Stage decisions should use the complete epoch and channel context. Electrode-related drift should not be allowed to masquerade as physiologic slow-wave activity.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate technical response?
options: Assess the patient and electrode environment, inspect affected electrodes, and correct the source when feasible
Score N3 immediately because the waveform is slow
Remove all frontal channels from the montage
Increase sensitivity until the drift looks smaller
questions.answer: Assess the patient and electrode environment, inspect affected electrodes, and correct the source when feasible
questions.rationale: The technologist should identify and correct the source rather than adapting scoring to an artifact-contaminated signal.

questions.prompt: C3-M2 contains a dense, regular high-frequency pattern that is not present in neighboring EEG channels. What is the most likely artifact family?
questions.rationale: A regular high-frequency pattern isolated to a signal pathway should prompt an electrical/electrode troubleshooting sequence rather than physiologic interpretation.

questions.prompt: Which channel is most affected by the regular interference?
questions.rationale: The schematic interference is intentionally concentrated in C3-M2.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before relying on filter changes?
options: Electrode impedance/contact, reference/ground pathway, cables, and nearby electrical sources
questions.answer: Electrode impedance/contact, reference/ground pathway, cables, and nearby electrical sources
questions.rationale: Troubleshoot the acquisition pathway first. Filters can alter clinically useful signal content and should not substitute for correcting an avoidable technical source.

questions.prompt: An irregular burst appears at the same time in F3-M2, C3-M2, E1-M2, and E2-M2, while F4-M1, C4-M1, Chin EMG, and ECG remain comparatively stable. What is the best explanation?
options: Artifact introduced through the shared M2 reference
Generalized body movement affecting all bioelectric channels
questions.answer: Artifact introduced through the shared M2 reference
questions.rationale: The disturbed derivations all use M2, while M1-referenced EEG and the separate bipolar chin EMG remain stable. That channel distribution points to the shared reference pathway rather than generalized movement.

questions.prompt: Which observation most strongly supports a shared-reference source?
options: Only derivations using M2 share the disturbance while M1-referenced EEG and Chin EMG remain stable
Every displayed bioelectric channel changes together
Only the ECG complexes become larger
The artifact appears only when SpO2 decreases
questions.answer: Only derivations using M2 share the disturbance while M1-referenced EEG and Chin EMG remain stable
questions.rationale: A common reference can distribute one unwanted signal into every derivation that uses that reference. Stable channels that do not use M2 help localize the source.

questions.prompt: What is the best next technologist response to this shared M2 reference disturbance?
options: Inspect and secure M2, verify its contact and impedance, then confirm the affected derivations recover
Reapply the chin EMG electrodes first because the chin channel is stable
Score the disturbance as cerebral activity
Turn off all M2-referenced channels for the remainder of the study
questions.answer: Inspect and secure M2, verify its contact and impedance, then confirm the affected derivations recover
questions.rationale: Troubleshooting should follow the shared signal pathway. When several derivations using one reference are affected together, inspect that reference and confirm signal recovery after correction.
